overview: This file brings together two groups of records on Japanese wireless regulation. The 1931 documents concern rules allowing foreign diplomatic missions in Japan to install receiving-only short-wave and long-distance radio equipment on a reciprocal basis, followed by State Department circulation of the rules and confirmation that Japanese diplomats could operate receivers in Washington without prior authorization. The 1938 despatch and its five enclosures document a coordinated revision of Japanese wireless-telegram regulations governing maritime medical-treatment messages, including their legal classification, reduced tariffs, operating signals, and a designated network of seamen’s hospitals in major Japanese ports.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 359 on radio receivers at diplomatic missions
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville forwards Japanese regulations governing diplomatic missions’ installation and use of radio receiving equipment and requests information on corresponding U.S. restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports that the Japanese circular permits diplomatic missions to install only receiving sets and makes authorization dependent on reciprocity. He asks what restrictions, if any, the United States imposes on diplomatic missions and encloses a translation of the circular.

subfiles.title: French text of Japanese diplomatic radio circular
subfiles.from: Imperial Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Foreign embassies and legations in Japan
subfiles.about: The circular sets conditions under which diplomatic missions may install short-wave and long-distance radio receivers.
subfiles.summary: The French text permits equipment used exclusively to receive public broadcasts, subject to reciprocity with the mission chief’s country. Applications must pass through the Foreign Ministry and identify the installer, location, apparatus, stations, countries, and desired broadcasts. Material received through authorized installations may not be reproduced in newspapers or periodicals.

subfiles.title: English translation of Japanese diplomatic radio circular
subfiles.from: Imperial Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Foreign embassies and legations in Japan
subfiles.about: The English translation states the licensing, reciprocity, application, and publication rules for diplomatic radio receivers.
subfiles.summary: Diplomatic installations are limited to reception of public broadcasts and may use no more power than necessary, with permission conditioned on reciprocity. Mission chiefs must apply through the Foreign Ministry to the Ministry of Communications and provide technical and programming information. Newspapers and periodicals are forbidden to reproduce content received through the authorized equipment.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japanese radio circular to the Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The State Department transmits the Japanese diplomatic radio circular to the Navy Department.
subfiles.summary: The note forwards a translation received from the American Embassy at Tokyo. It identifies the subject as the installation of broadcast receiving sets by diplomatic missions in Japan.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japanese radio circular to the Federal Radio Commission
subfiles.to: The Chairman of the Federal Radio Commission
subfiles.about: The State Department sends the Federal Radio Commission the Japanese rules for diplomatic broadcast receivers.
subfiles.summary: The note transmits a translation of the circular received from the American Embassy at Tokyo. Its purpose is to inform the federal radio regulator about Japanese restrictions on diplomatic missions’ receiving sets.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japanese radio circular to the Secretary of War
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards the Japanese diplomatic radio circular to the War Department.
subfiles.summary: The note supplies the Secretary of War with a translation received from the American Embassy in Tokyo. It concerns Japanese regulation of broadcast receiving equipment installed by diplomatic missions.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 217 on U.S. treatment of diplomatic radio receivers
subfiles.from: The Secretary of State, signed by William R. Castle Jr.
subfiles.to: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The State Department authorizes Forbes to tell Japan that the United States requires no prior permission for diplomatic broadcast receivers.
subfiles.summary: Responding to Despatch No. 359, the Department states that U.S. authorities require no advance permission to install broadcast receiving sets. It specifically raises no objection to the Japanese Embassy in Washington installing and using either short-wave or long-wave receivers.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3127 transmitting revised wireless-telegram regulations
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew forwards five translations concerning Japan’s revised regulation of medical-treatment wireless telegrams.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy transmits recent ordinances and announcements revising Japanese wireless-telegram regulations. The revisions govern messages seeking medical advice for sick or injured persons aboard ships. Grew also encloses a translated list of Japanese hospitals authorized to send and receive such telegrams.

subfiles.title: Ordinance No. 40 revising domestic wireless-telegram regulations
subfiles.about: Ordinance No. 40 defines medical-treatment wireless telegrams and establishes their procedures and charges.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance classifies ship captains’ requests for medical instructions, and the replies from designated hospitals or doctor-carrying ships, as medical-treatment telegrams. Senders must mark the telegram form “medical treatment.” It also revises the charging schedule and provides reduced rates for these messages, effective June 1, 1938.

subfiles.title: Ordinance No. 43 revising foreign wireless-telegram regulations
subfiles.about: Ordinance No. 43 reduces rates and defines international medical-treatment wireless messages involving Japanese and foreign ships and hospitals.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance establishes medical-message rates of 12 sen per word at land stations and 8 sen per word at movable stations, half the regular rates stated in the document. It recognizes exchanges between Japanese ship captains and authorized foreign hospitals or doctor-carrying foreign ships, as well as exchanges between foreign captains and designated Japanese hospitals or ships. Senders must mark the message “medical treatment,” and the changes take effect June 1, 1938.

subfiles.title: Ordinance No. 42 on handling private communications
subfiles.about: Ordinance No. 42 adds medical-treatment wireless telegrams to regulations for handling private telegraphic communications.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance revises rules covering private telegrams, private wireless telegrams, and public communications. It inserts wireless telegrams for medical treatment into the relevant regulatory provision, effective June 1, 1938.

subfiles.title: Ordinance No. 41 prescribing medical-treatment radio signals
subfiles.to: Private wireless telegraph and telephone operators
subfiles.about: Ordinance No. 41 prescribes the coded calling sequence and spoken labels used when ships seek medical assistance by wireless.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance instructs operators of private shipboard wireless equipment how to call government telegraph offices or ships carrying doctors. It specifies a medical-treatment signal, introductory signal, self-call signal, and transmission-demand signal, and adds medical-treatment terminology to the regulated safety and introductory signals. The effective date is June 1, 1938; the OCR’s “1958” is an evident error.

subfiles.title: Announcement No. 1432 listing designated medical-telegram hospitals
subfiles.about: The announcement identifies five Japanese seamen’s hospitals authorized to send and receive medical-treatment wireless telegrams.
subfiles.summary: The designated facilities are the Japan Seamen’s Relief Association hospitals at Yokohama, Osaka, Kobe, Moji, and Nagasaki. The table supplies each hospital’s street address, domestic telegram address, and European-format address beginning with KKEB. The designation becomes effective June 1, 1938.

interest: The file is valuable for showing how radio policy connected diplomatic privilege, reciprocity, censorship, and interdepartmental administration in the early 1930s. Its 1938 enclosures provide unusually concrete evidence for an early maritime telemedicine system: reduced tariffs, standardized emergency calling signals, rules for international exchanges, and a port-by-port hospital network. The bilingual 1931 circular, internal distribution notes, technical rate schedules, and precise telegraph addresses make the bundle useful for diplomatic, communications, maritime, medical, and infrastructural history.
